title: Looking back: tellers and saints
hookLine: Bhai Gurdas, the janamsakhis and fifteen Bhagats

lines: A SCRIBE, A STORYTELLER, A WEAVER.
cards: Every story you've heard this year reached you because somebody told it first. A scribe bent over a page with a reed pen. A storyteller in a village courtyard, saying, and then Baba Nanak went on to the next town.
A weaver at his loom, singing to God, whose song ended up in the Guru's own book. Before the battles and the kingdoms, year three began with these people, the ones who carried the story.
For the last days of the year, this path turns around to look at the road. First, the tellers and the saints.

teach.h: THE SCRIBE: BHAI GURDAS AND HIS VARS.
teach.b: Start with the scribe. Tradition says Bhai Gurdas wrote out the Adi Granth in his own hand for Guru Arjan. He also wrote vars of his own: long poems in pauris, each with a picture and a point.

He tells Nanak's journeys, the yogis on the mountain, the qazis at Mecca, the Guru laying down the pilgrim's robe to live as a householder. Tradition says Guru Arjan called those vars the key to the Guru's word.
Next, the storytellers. The janamsakhis, the birth-stories of Nanak, came down in more than one family of tellings: the Puratan, the Bala, Miharban's reflective version, an illustrated one.

They don't always agree on the details. Some readers take them as memory and devotion more than as diaries, and that's part of what they teach: a life so loved that people kept telling it, each in their own voice.

teach.h: THE SAINTS: BHAGATS IN THE GURU'S BOOK.
teach.b: Then the saints. At the end of the ragas in the Guru Granth Sahib sit the hymns of the Bhagats. Kabir.
Shaikh Farid, the Sufi. Namdev. Ravidas, who in his own hymns names the low caste he was born into and says the Name lifted him anyway.
Dhanna the farmer, Sain the barber, and others. They came from many places and castes, from Hindu and Muslim backgrounds, and the Gurus set their words beside their own.

teach.h: THE WORD TRAVELS IN HUMAN HANDS.
teach.b: One shape runs through all three: the Gurus' word didn't travel alone. It traveled in the hands of people who wrote, retold and sang it.

how: Sikhs hear the vars of Bhai Gurdas sung in kirtan alongside Gurbani, retell the janamsakhi stories of Guru Nanak at gurpurabs and to children, and sing the Bhagats' hymns from the Guru Granth Sahib as part of the Guru's word.

o: regret for mistakes the Sikhs once made
a call to go back to the old village ways
seeing who carried the Gurus' word down to us

games.q: the tellers of year three — tap the pairs.
p: wrote out the Adi Granth for Guru Arjan

s: every janamsakhi tells Nanak's life the same way

the Guru Granth Sahib holds hymns by saints who were not Sikh Gurus

games.q: you are compiling a holy book for your community. the hymns of saints from other castes and backgrounds are in front of you. what do you do?
o: leave them out to keep the book only your own.
set their hymns inside the book beside your own.
keep them in a separate appendix nobody reads.
games.why: the Bhagats' hymns sit inside the Guru Granth Sahib itself, at the end of the ragas, among the Gurus' own words.

practice: Let one teller from this year step forward: the scribe with his careful pen, Bhai Nand Lal with his Persian verses of longing, Kabir at the loom, Farid, or the unnamed people who first said, and then Baba Nanak went on.
Hold that person in mind for a few breaths, and say their name quietly. If you pray, say Waheguru in thanks for them on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Looking back. Turning at the end of the year to see the road: today, the scribe, the storytellers and the saints whose words sit in the Guru's book. Today's word.

orig.note: bhagat, a devotee: the word for the saints whose hymns sit in the Guru Granth Sahib.

carryVoice: Your line: the tellers. A story lives as long as someone keeps telling it. Thanks for sitting with me.
